Model Response:

The Case for Abolishing Taxation and Funding Society Voluntarily

Taxation is commonly presented as an unavoidable feature of civilized life. Governments insist that roads, schools, courts, emergency services, infrastructure, and national defense can exist only if citizens are compelled to surrender a portion of their income and property. Yet this claim rests on an assumption that deserves far greater scrutiny: that the state has a moral right to take resources from people without their individual consent.

A principled defense of liberty should reject that assumption. Taxation is not fundamentally different from compelled payment enforced through legal threats. If an ordinary person demanded money from a neighbor under threat of fines, asset seizure, imprisonment, or other punishment, society would call it extortion or theft. The fact that the demand is made by an institution called “government” does not automatically transform coercion into a moral act. A society committed to consent, property rights, and human dignity should therefore seek the complete abolition of compulsory taxation and replace it with voluntary, contractual, charitable, cooperative, and private methods of funding services.

Taxation Is Coercion, Not Consent

The defining feature of taxation is compulsion. Citizens do not choose whether to pay; they may choose only how much legal risk they are willing to accept in resisting payment. Failure to comply can result in penalties, wage garnishment, property liens, confiscation, license suspension, and, in extreme cases, imprisonment. This is not voluntary cooperation. It is a financial obligation enforced by the state’s monopoly on legal force.

Supporters of taxation often argue that people “consent” merely by living within a country’s borders, using public roads, voting, or accepting the benefits of public institutions. But this is a weak definition of consent. Most people are born into a political jurisdiction rather than freely joining it. Moving away may be financially impossible, socially devastating, or legally complicated. Voting does not solve the problem either: casting a ballot does not mean one has agreed to every policy enacted by the winning coalition. A person who votes against a tax, or does not vote at all, is still required to pay it.

Genuine consent requires the meaningful ability to refuse. In ordinary life, a person may decline to buy a product, hire a service, join a club, donate to a charity, or sign a contract. Under taxation, refusal is punished. The arrangement is therefore not consensual in the moral sense, regardless of whether it is legal under existing law.

Property Rights Cannot Be Taken Seriously If Taxation Is Treated as Normal

A free society depends on the recognition that individuals have rightful claims to the fruits of their labor, creativity, savings, and voluntary exchange. People work, build businesses, take risks, acquire skills, and save money partly because they expect to retain the resources they earn. Taxation weakens that expectation by asserting that the state has a prior claim on every paycheck, transaction, inheritance, investment, and possession.

When governments tax income, they take a portion of a person’s labor. When they tax property, they impose an ongoing payment simply for retaining what one already owns. When they tax sales, they raise the price of ordinary exchange. When they tax investment and savings, they penalize prudence and long-term planning. When they tax inheritance, they reach even beyond death, claiming a share of property that has already been earned and often taxed multiple times.

Defenders of taxation may respond that property rights are themselves created or protected by the state. But this reverses the moral order. Governments may help enforce property claims, yet the fact that an institution provides a service does not entitle it to seize unlimited payment from those it serves. A security company that protects a home would not thereby gain the right to enter that home and take whatever it wishes. A court system that resolves disputes does not gain moral ownership over the wealth of everyone under its jurisdiction.

If individuals have a right to peaceful possession and voluntary exchange, then the burden falls on advocates of taxation to explain why that right may be overridden by force. Invoking “the public good” is not enough. Nearly any coercive policy can be defended with appeals to collective benefit. A moral society must ask not only whether a program has admirable goals, but whether it is legitimate to compel unwilling people to pay for it.

Taxation Encourages Waste, Political Favoritism, and Irresponsibility

Even if one sets aside the moral objection to coercion, taxation creates serious practical problems. Governments spend money differently from individuals, families, charities, and competitive businesses because public officials do not bear the same consequences for waste. When a private company wastes resources, it risks losing customers, investors, and market share. When a government agency wastes resources, it often receives a larger budget, more authority, or new justifications for continued funding.

Tax revenue also encourages political favoritism. Once the state has access to vast compulsory revenues, powerful interest groups have an incentive to lobby for subsidies, contracts, exemptions, bailouts, special regulations, and targeted benefits. Businesses and industries that should compete by serving consumers instead compete for political influence. Citizens are transformed from voluntary participants in a marketplace into factions fighting over access to other people’s money.

A tax-funded state also obscures the real cost of public services. People may support programs when they appear “free,” but those programs are never actually free; their costs are dispersed through payroll deductions, sales taxes, inflationary financing, debt, and hidden fees. The result is a culture in which citizens demand ever more services while rarely confronting the full price of what they demand.

Voluntary funding would create greater transparency. If people had to choose directly whether to support a service, organizations would need to demonstrate their value. Providers would have stronger incentives to become efficient, responsive, and trustworthy. Poorly run institutions would lose support; successful ones would earn it.

Voluntary Alternatives Are More Realistic Than Critics Admit

The most common objection to abolishing taxation is that essential public services would collapse. Yet this assumes that government monopoly and compulsory funding are the only means by which people can cooperate on large-scale needs. History and modern practice show otherwise.

Many vital services are already provided wholly or partly through voluntary arrangements. Private businesses construct and maintain buildings, transportation networks, communications systems, hospitals, utility systems, research laboratories, and logistics chains of enormous complexity. Charities fund food assistance, medical care, education, disaster relief, housing support, cultural institutions, and community programs. Mutual-aid societies have historically helped workers and families obtain insurance, health care, burial benefits, disability support, and emergency assistance without centralized state control.

A society without taxation could fund services through a broad range of voluntary mechanisms:

  • Direct user fees: People pay for services they use, such as roads, transit, utilities, courts, or recreational facilities.
  • Private subscriptions: Individuals and businesses pay regular fees for security, emergency response, infrastructure maintenance, or community services.
  • Cooperatives: Residents, workers, or businesses jointly own and finance local services, distributing costs through voluntary membership agreements.
  • Insurance markets: Insurance providers could fund fire protection, dispute resolution, health services, risk prevention, and emergency response because reducing harm benefits both insurers and policyholders.
  • Charitable organizations: Philanthropy and community giving could support services for people unable to pay.
  • Business sponsorship and investment: Firms have strong incentives to support safe neighborhoods, reliable infrastructure, educated workers, and stable commercial environments.
  • Covenant communities and contractual associations: Neighborhoods and local communities could establish rules and service packages through explicit agreements rather than compulsory taxation imposed from above.
  • Crowdfunding and voluntary bonds: Large projects could be financed by investors and donors who expect either financial returns, social benefits, or both.

None of these mechanisms is perfect, but neither is taxation. The relevant comparison is not between an ideal tax-funded state and a chaotic imaginary alternative. It is between compulsory systems that concentrate power and voluntary systems that must earn support.

Public Goods Do Not Justify Unlimited Coercion

Critics frequently argue that certain “public goods,” especially national defense, policing, courts, and infrastructure, cannot be funded voluntarily because people may try to benefit without paying. This concern deserves consideration, but it does not establish that coercion is morally justified.

First, people often voluntarily contribute to goods from which others may benefit. They donate to disaster relief, libraries, scientific research, environmental protection, public broadcasting, religious institutions, local parks, and neighborhood improvement projects. Human beings are not purely self-interested calculators. They are motivated by compassion, reputation, community loyalty, moral principle, religious conviction, business interest, and personal pride.

Second, many supposed public goods can be structured so that benefits are linked to payment. Roads can use tolls, subscriptions, electronic access systems, or commercial partnerships. Security can be funded through insurers, neighborhood associations, businesses, and voluntary contracts. Arbitration and private dispute-resolution systems can compete on quality, speed, and fairness. Infrastructure can be financed through investment, usage charges, and property-development agreements.

Third, even where free-rider problems remain, they do not erase the ethical problem of compelled payment. The possibility that some people may benefit without contributing does not give others a blanket right to seize their resources. A moral society should seek persuasive, contractual, and cooperative solutions before resorting to force.

Voluntary Funding Would Strengthen Civil Society

One of the most damaging effects of taxation is that it encourages citizens to outsource moral responsibility to the state. People may conclude that because they pay taxes, they have fulfilled their obligations to the poor, the sick, the elderly, the vulnerable, and their communities. Yet writing a compulsory check to the government is not the same as practicing generosity, solidarity, or civic responsibility.

A voluntary society would require stronger communities. Families, religious organizations, charities, mutual-aid associations, local cooperatives, businesses, and neighborhood groups would become more central to everyday life. Such institutions are often more personal and accountable than distant bureaucracies. They can adapt more easily to local conditions, identify genuine needs, and treat people as individuals rather than as case numbers in a centralized system.

This does not mean voluntary institutions would always be generous or effective. Human beings and organizations can fail in any system. But voluntary arrangements retain an essential moral advantage: they respect the agency of those who give and those who receive. They allow people to choose causes, evaluate providers, demand accountability, and build relationships based on cooperation rather than compulsion.

Abolition Is a Moral Direction, Not a Call for Disorder

Advocating the abolition of taxation need not mean demanding reckless overnight dismantling of every existing public institution. A transition away from taxation could be gradual and orderly. Governments could reduce spending, privatize functions that can be competitively provided, repeal punitive and distortionary taxes, transfer assets to community trusts or user cooperatives, and encourage voluntary alternatives to expand.

The central principle is that no service should be presumed entitled to funding through coercion. Every institution should have to justify itself to the people it serves. If a road, hospital, school, court, emergency service, or security provider is valuable, then individuals and communities should be free to support it openly and voluntarily. If an institution cannot persuade people to fund it, that should prompt reform, competition, or reconsideration—not a greater resort to force.

Conclusion

Taxation is often defended as practical, traditional, or necessary. But tradition does not establish legitimacy, convenience does not establish morality, and claims of necessity should not excuse permanent violations of individual rights. At its core, taxation rests on the assertion that the state may take property from peaceful people because it believes it can spend that property better or more broadly than they can.

That assertion is incompatible with a robust commitment to consent and liberty. A society that condemns theft in private life should not celebrate it when performed through political institutions. The more consistent alternative is to abolish compulsory taxation and replace it with voluntary exchange, contractual association, private enterprise, mutual aid, philanthropy, insurance, cooperative ownership, and community initiative.

The goal should not be a society with no services, no solidarity, or no shared projects. It should be a society in which those things arise through persuasion rather than compulsion; through consent rather than confiscation; and through free people working together rather than being forced to fund institutions they did not choose.

From the viewpoint that taxation is unethical coercion, abolishing all taxes is seen as both a moral requirement and a practical way to create a freer, more efficient society. This perspective is commonly associated with anarcho-capitalism, radical libertarianism, and some voluntaryist theories.

Core moral argument: taxation is compulsory taking

The central claim is that taxes are not genuinely voluntary. Individuals must pay them under threat of penalties, asset seizure, fines, imprisonment, or other legal sanctions. From this view, calling taxation a “social contribution” does not change its coercive character, because consent is absent.

Supporters often argue:

  • People have a right to the income and property they acquire peacefully.
  • Taking a portion of that property without consent is morally similar to theft, even when done by government.
  • A democratic vote does not make coercion ethical; a majority should not gain the right to seize a minority’s property merely by voting.
  • Government services funded through taxation are therefore funded by compelled rather than voluntary payment.

In this framework, abolishing taxation is primarily about respecting individual self-ownership, property rights, and freedom of association.

Consent-based funding instead of tax funding

Advocates of a tax-free society propose that services now funded through taxes could instead be paid for voluntarily. Possible mechanisms include:

  • Direct user fees, such as tolls or subscription charges.
  • Private charities and mutual-aid societies.
  • Voluntary donations and crowdfunding.
  • Private insurance, including insurance for security, health, disaster relief, or legal disputes.
  • Membership organizations, cooperatives, and neighborhood associations.
  • Businesses funding infrastructure or services that help their customers and employees.
  • Endowments, philanthropy, and nonprofit institutions.

The claimed advantage is that people would support only the services they value, rather than being required to fund programs they oppose or do not use.

Greater personal freedom and control over income

Abolishing taxes would, in this view, let people retain all of their earnings and decide for themselves how to spend, save, invest, donate, or insure it.

Supporters argue that this would:

  • Increase individual autonomy.
  • Allow families and communities to prioritize their own needs.
  • Reduce dependence on political decisions.
  • Make charitable giving more intentional and locally responsive.
  • Enable people to avoid financing wars, corporate subsidies, surveillance, prisons, or other government activities they find objectionable.

The idea is that private individuals, not government agencies, should decide what causes and services deserve resources.

Reduced government power and abuse

Anti-tax advocates often see taxation as the financial foundation of an excessively powerful state. If government can compel revenue, it can expand programs, regulations, military operations, surveillance, and political patronage without needing ongoing voluntary approval from those who fund it.

They argue that ending taxation would:

  • Limit the size and scope of government.
  • Reduce incentives for political lobbying and rent-seeking.
  • Make it harder for officials to fund wars or unpopular policies.
  • Reduce corruption associated with public budgets and contracts.
  • Prevent politicians from redistributing wealth to favored groups.
  • Force institutions to earn support rather than rely on compulsory revenue.

Under this view, voluntary financing acts as a discipline: organizations that fail to serve people well lose customers, donors, or members.

Better economic efficiency and innovation

Advocates claim taxes distort economic choices. Income taxes may discourage work and saving; corporate taxes may reduce investment; sales taxes may discourage exchange; payroll taxes may raise the cost of hiring; and complex tax codes can consume time and money through accounting, compliance, and legal disputes.

They believe a tax-free system could produce benefits such as:

  • More investment and entrepreneurship.
  • Higher take-home pay.
  • Lower administrative and compliance costs.
  • Fewer resources spent on tax lawyers, audits, reporting, and enforcement.
  • More competition among providers of services.
  • Greater experimentation with different business and community models.

For example, rather than one tax-funded road authority, private operators, local associations, developers, or businesses might experiment with tolls, subscriptions, bundled services, or other arrangements.

Competition instead of monopoly provision

This perspective often treats government as a monopoly provider funded regardless of customer satisfaction. Because taxpayers cannot easily opt out, advocates argue that public agencies may face weaker incentives to reduce costs, improve quality, or respond to users.

Voluntary private alternatives are expected to create competitive pressure. In theory:

  • Consumers can choose among providers.
  • Poor providers lose customers.
  • Successful models expand.
  • Prices and quality are shaped by demand rather than political bargaining.
  • Services can be tailored to different communities rather than standardized nationally.

This argument is applied not only to ordinary services but, in more radical versions, to policing, courts, roads, education, welfare, emergency response, and national defense.

Voluntary charity and mutual aid as alternatives to welfare taxation

Supporters frequently argue that compulsory welfare programs displace voluntary generosity and weaken local community responsibility. They point to historical examples of mutual-aid societies, religious charities, fraternal organizations, community funds, and private hospitals.

They contend that voluntary assistance could be:

  • More personal and responsive.
  • Less bureaucratic.
  • Better able to distinguish genuine need from fraud.
  • More connected to local circumstances.
  • Less likely to create long-term dependency.
  • More respectful because aid is offered through willing cooperation rather than political compulsion.

The ideal is not necessarily indifference to poverty; rather, it is assistance organized through voluntary relationships rather than tax-funded redistribution.

Accountability through voluntary payment

A central practical claim is that voluntary funding creates clearer accountability. If people must willingly pay, donate, subscribe, or join, service providers must persuade them that the service is worthwhile.

This is thought to discourage waste because:

  • Revenue depends on continued satisfaction.
  • Donors and customers can withdraw support.
  • Funding decisions are decentralized.
  • People can compare alternatives.
  • Providers have incentives to show results.

Tax-funded agencies, by contrast, are said to receive money regardless of whether individual taxpayers approve of their performance.

Important qualification: these are contested claims

The above is the case made from the anti-coercive, voluntaryist perspective. Critics challenge it on several grounds, especially the risk that essential but unprofitable services would be undersupplied. They question whether voluntary funding could reliably provide public goods such as national defense, epidemic control, courts, environmental protection, universal infrastructure, and support for people with severe disabilities or no ability to pay.

Critics also argue that private provision can produce unequal access, private monopolies, weak democratic accountability, and free-rider problems. Supporters of abolishing taxation reply that such problems are often worsened by state systems and that voluntary institutions, markets, insurance, contracts, charities, and local associations could develop alternatives.

So, in its strongest form, the tax-abolition position rests on two linked ideas: compulsory taxation is morally illegitimate because it violates consent, and voluntary institutions would be more ethical, accountable, adaptable, and economically efficient than government systems funded by force.

The Case for the Complete Abolition of Taxation: A Call for Voluntary Society

Introduction

Taxation is one of the most pervasive and oppressive mechanisms of state power in modern society. Far from being a necessary evil for public goods, taxation is fundamentally an act of coercion—legalized theft by the state that distorts markets, stifles innovation, and undermines individual liberty. The idea that citizens must surrender a portion of their earnings to the government under threat of punishment is not only unjust but also economically inefficient. A society that rejects taxation in favor of voluntary contributions and private provision of services would be far more prosperous, free, and just. This essay argues that taxation is illegitimate state theft, that voluntary alternatives are both feasible and superior, and that the abolition of all taxes would lead to a more dynamic, ethical, and flourishing civilization.

Taxation is State Theft: A Moral and Legal Violation

1. The Coercive Nature of Taxation

Taxation is not a voluntary exchange but a forced transfer of wealth. Unlike voluntary donations, taxes are imposed by law, meaning that refusal results in penalties—fines, asset seizures, imprisonment, or even deportation. This is not taxation; it is legalized robbery. The state claims the right to take a portion of one’s income or property without consent, under the pretense of "public necessity." But necessity does not justify theft—if it did, every dictator could justify their crimes as "necessary for stability."

Historically, taxation has been used as a tool of oppression. The British taxed the American colonies without representation, sparking the American Revolution. The French nobility imposed heavy taxes on the peasantry, contributing to the French Revolution. Today, high taxation in countries like Sweden and Denmark has led to economic stagnation and mass emigration. If taxation is truly necessary for a functioning society, why do so many people flee high-tax jurisdictions in search of freedom?

2. The Slippery Slope of "Public Good" Justifications

Proponents of taxation argue that it funds essential services—defense, infrastructure, education, healthcare, and social welfare. However, this reasoning is flawed on multiple levels.

First, no government has a monopoly on providing these services. Private companies, charities, and community organizations have successfully delivered education, healthcare, and infrastructure for centuries. The Catholic Church, for example, has run schools and hospitals for millennia without taxation. The modern welfare state is not a natural evolution of human cooperation but a relatively recent experiment that has proven costly and inefficient.

Second, taxation distorts priorities. When the state controls funding, it inevitably favors politically connected interests over those that would emerge from free-market competition. Subsidies for failing industries, crony capitalism, and bureaucratic waste are all byproducts of state-controlled finance. Voluntary contributions, by contrast, allow individuals to direct resources toward causes they genuinely support.

Third, the "public good" is an illusion. The state claims to act in the collective interest, but in reality, it serves the interests of those in power. Taxation is not about fairness—it is about control. The more the state takes, the more it can manipulate, regulate, and suppress dissent.

3. The Hypocrisy of "Progressive" Taxation

The Case for the Abolition of Taxation: Ending State Theft and Embracing Voluntary Funding

Taxation, often regarded as the bedrock of modern government, is fundamentally an act of coercion that undermines individual liberty and moral principles. Defined as the mandatory extraction of resources from individuals and businesses by the state, taxation is, at its core, a form of legalized theft. It is imposed without explicit consent, often under the threat of violence or imprisonment, and redistributes wealth in ways that may not align with the payer's values or priorities. This essay argues emphatically for the complete abolition of all forms of taxation, contending that it is an illegitimate exercise of state power and advocating for a system of purely voluntary or private funding for all public services. Such a paradigm shift would not only restore individual autonomy but also foster a more just, efficient, and morally sound society.

Taxation as State Theft

The moral argument against taxation rests on the principle of property rights, a cornerstone of individual freedom. Property, whether in the form of income, assets, or labor, is the product of an individual's effort, ingenuity, and time. When the state forcibly seizes a portion of this property through taxation, it violates the fundamental right to ownership. Philosopher Robert Nozick famously likened taxation to forced labor, arguing that taking the fruits of one’s work without consent is akin to partial enslavement. If an individual does not voluntarily agree to surrender their earnings, the act of taxation becomes indistinguishable from theft, regardless of the state’s purported intentions.

Proponents of taxation often justify it as a "social contract"—an implicit agreement between citizens and the state to fund collective goods. However, this concept is deeply flawed. A true contract requires explicit consent, mutual agreement, and the ability to opt out. Taxation offers none of these. Citizens are born into a system of compulsory payment, with no opportunity to negotiate terms or refuse participation without severe consequences, such as fines or incarceration. This lack of choice renders the social contract a fiction, a post hoc rationalization for state coercion. If a private individual or organization demanded payment under threat of violence, it would be universally condemned as extortion. The state’s monopoly on force does not morally legitimize such behavior; it merely masks it under the guise of legality.

The Inefficiency and Injustice of Taxation

Beyond its moral failings, taxation is a deeply inefficient and unjust mechanism for funding public services. Governments, lacking the profit motive and competitive pressures of the private sector, often mismanage taxpayer funds through bureaucratic waste, corruption, and poorly prioritized spending. In the United States, for instance, the Government Accountability Office reported in 2022 that federal agencies made over $247 billion in improper payments—money lost to fraud, errors, or inefficiency. Such staggering figures are not anomalies but systemic outcomes of a structure unaccountable to market forces or individual choice. If public services were funded voluntarily, providers would be incentivized to minimize waste and maximize value to attract contributions, much like businesses must satisfy customers to survive.

Moreover, taxation disproportionately burdens certain groups while benefiting others, creating inequities that undermine social cohesion. Progressive income taxes, for example, penalize success by extracting a higher percentage of earnings from the wealthy, often to fund programs that may not directly benefit them. Conversely, regressive taxes like sales taxes disproportionately harm low-income individuals, for whom basic purchases consume a larger share of their income. Tax loopholes and exemptions further exacerbate inequality, as powerful corporations and well-connected individuals often evade their "fair share" while ordinary citizens bear the brunt. A voluntary funding model would eliminate these disparities, allowing individuals to support only the causes and services they value, without the state arbitrarily deciding who pays and who benefits.

The Viability of Voluntary and Private Funding

Critics of abolishing taxation often argue that public services—such as infrastructure, education, healthcare, and defense—cannot be adequately funded without compulsory contributions. This assumption underestimates both human ingenuity and the power of voluntary cooperation. History and contemporary examples demonstrate that communities can and do organize to meet collective needs without coercion. Mutual aid societies, private charities, and crowdfunding platforms have long provided safety nets and public goods, often more efficiently than government programs. For instance, during the 19th century, before the advent of widespread taxation for social welfare, fraternal organizations in the United States provided insurance, healthcare, and support to millions of members through voluntary contributions.

In a post-taxation world, public services could be funded through a combination of user fees, donations, and private investment. Roads and infrastructure, for example, could operate on a toll or subscription basis, with private companies competing to offer the best quality at the lowest cost. Education could be provided by private institutions or community cooperatives, with scholarships and crowdfunding ensuring access for the disadvantaged. Defense, often cited as the quintessential public good, could be financed through voluntary contributions or mutual defense agreements, as individuals and businesses have a vested interest in protecting their property and freedoms. Blockchain technology and smart contracts could further facilitate transparent, decentralized funding mechanisms, ensuring that contributions are allocated as intended without the need for a coercive intermediary.

Skeptics may argue that voluntary funding risks underprovision of essential services, as some individuals might "free ride" by benefiting without contributing. However, social norms, reputation incentives, and innovative funding models can mitigate this concern. People are more likely to contribute when they see direct benefits, trust the system, and feel a sense of personal agency—conditions far more achievable in a voluntary framework than under compulsory taxation. Additionally, private entities have a proven track record of addressing collective needs when given the opportunity. For instance, private security firms and neighborhood associations already supplement or replace state-provided policing in many areas, often with greater accountability to their clients.

Restoring Liberty and Accountability

The abolition of taxation would not only dismantle an unjust system but also fundamentally transform the relationship between individuals and the state. By replacing coercion with choice, society would shift toward a model of governance based on consent and mutual benefit. Governments, stripped of their power to extract resources by force, would be compelled to justify their existence through value creation, much like any other service provider. This would foster a culture of accountability, as public entities could no longer rely on guaranteed revenue but would instead need to earn the trust and support of citizens.

Furthermore, the elimination of taxation would unleash economic potential by allowing individuals to retain the full fruits of their labor. Without the burden of income, property, or sales taxes, people would have greater disposable income to save, invest, or spend as they see fit, driving innovation and prosperity. Small businesses, often stifled by complex tax codes and compliance costs, would thrive in an environment free from such constraints. The resulting economic dynamism would create a virtuous cycle, generating more resources for voluntary contributions to public goods.

Addressing Counterarguments

Opponents of abolishing taxation often warn of societal collapse, envisioning a world of crumbling infrastructure, rampant inequality, and unchecked crime. These fears, while understandable, are rooted in a lack of imagination and an overreliance on the status quo. The state’s monopoly on public services has conditioned us to believe that only centralized, coercive systems can address large-scale needs. Yet, as previously discussed, voluntary and private alternatives have repeatedly proven their efficacy when given the chance. Inequality, often exacerbated by state intervention through cronyism and poorly targeted redistribution, could be better addressed through direct, community-driven initiatives that empower individuals rather than paternalize them.

Another common critique is that voluntary funding would favor the wealthy, who could afford to contribute more and thus shape public services to their advantage. This concern overlooks the democratizing potential of collective action in a voluntary system. Crowdfunding and cooperative models allow even small contributions to aggregate into significant impact, ensuring that diverse voices are heard. Moreover, a free market for public goods would incentivize providers to cater to the broadest possible audience, not just the affluent, to maximize revenue.

Conclusion: A Call for Radical Freedom

Taxation, as it exists today, is an illegitimate act of state theft that violates individual rights, perpetuates inefficiency, and undermines justice. Its abolition is not a utopian fantasy but a moral and practical imperative. By transitioning to a system of voluntary and private funding for public services, we can restore personal liberty, foster economic vitality, and build a society grounded in consent rather than coercion. The path forward requires courage, creativity, and a willingness to challenge entrenched assumptions about the role of the state. But the reward—a world where individuals are truly free to shape their destinies and communities—is worth the effort. Let us reject the chains of taxation and embrace a future of radical freedom, where every contribution is a choice, not a command.

  1. Increased Individual Freedom:

  4. Market-Based Solutions and Competition:

Critiques and Challenges

While the idea of abolishing taxation has theoretical appeal to some, it faces significant practical and ethical challenges, which critics often highlight:

  • Public Goods Problem: Certain services, like national defense or clean air, are "public goods" that benefit everyone regardless of whether they pay. The viewpoint that taxation should be abolished stems from a deep commitment to individual liberty, property rights, and the belief that voluntary, private solutions are morally and practically superior to government coercion. However, the feasibility of replacing taxation entirely with voluntary mechanisms remains a subject of intense debate, as it requires addressing complex issues of public goods, equity, and societal coordination. The Theft of Consent: Why All Taxation Must Be Abolished and Replaced with Voluntary Public Service Funding

On a cold January morning in 2022, Maria Gonzalez, a single mother of two working 60 hours a week as a home health aide, found a garnishment notice in her mailbox. The state used its monopoly on force to seize the fruits of her labor without her explicit consent, punishing her for a crisis beyond her control. All taxation is illegitimate state theft that violates fundamental natural rights to property and consent, and voluntary or private funding mechanisms can deliver public services more efficiently, equitably, and morally than the coercive tax system we tolerate today.

The philosophical case against taxation rests on a bedrock of natural rights theory, most famously articulated by John Locke. Locke argued that each person has an inalienable right to the fruits of their labor: when a farmer tills a field, a nurse cares for a patient, or a teacher educates a child, they acquire a moral claim to the wages or goods they earn. Taxation, by contrast, is a form of coercion: the state demands a portion of that labor’s value under threat of violence. If a private individual broke into Maria’s home and stole 35% of her savings, we would call it theft and lock them in prison. When the IRS does the same—backed by SWAT teams, asset seizures, and criminal prosecution—it is labeled “tax collection.” This double standard is rooted in the state’s self-declared monopoly on force, not in any moral justification. The non-aggression principle (NAP), a cornerstone of libertarian ethics, amplifies this point: any action that initiates force against another person or their property is inherently wrong. Taxation is the ultimate initiation of force: it does not require explicit consent, it punishes those who cannot pay, and it prioritizes the state’s political agenda over the individual’s survival. Even progressive tax systems, lauded as “fair” by their proponents, are morally bankrupt: they punish productivity by seizing a larger share of income from those who work longer hours or take greater risks, while rewarding political cronyism by granting tax loopholes to corporations that lobby for favorable treatment.

Beyond its moral failure, taxation is a practical disaster. The U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO) estimates that $1.7 trillion in federal tax dollars was wasted on bureaucratic inefficiency, duplicate programs, and political pork barrel projects in 2023 alone—including a $2.2 billion “bridge to nowhere” in Alaska, $400 million in unused COVID-19 testing kits, and $100 million in subsidies for a private jet manufacturer that later declared bankruptcy. This waste is not an accident: tax dollars are allocated by politicians who prioritize re-election over public good, not by consumers who demand value for their money. Taxation also perpetuates systemic inequity: regressive sales taxes disproportionately harm low-income families who spend a larger share of their income on basic needs, while progressive income taxes punish small business owners who create 60% of new jobs in the U.S. Maria’s story is a perfect example: she paid a higher effective tax rate (including payroll and sales taxes) than her wealthy employer, who used a team of accountants to shelter $2 million in income in offshore accounts.   3. Enhanced Personal Choice
    Voluntary systems would allow individuals to prioritize their unique needs. A parent could allocate funds to a vocational school for their child instead of a public school with a one-size-fits-all curriculum; a retiree could invest in private long-term care instead of contributing to a state pension system they may not rely on.

Mainstream economists, policymakers, and ethicists widely reject this perspective due to significant practical and moral flaws:

  • Free-Rider Problem: Voluntary funding for non-excludable public goods (e.g., national defense) would likely fail, as individuals could benefit without contributing (the "free-rider" problem), leading to underprovision of essential services.
  • Inequity and Lack of Access: Low-income individuals would be unable to afford private services (e.g., healthcare, education), exacerbating inequality and creating a two-tier system for the wealthy and marginalized.

In summary, while the perspective that taxation is unethical coercion and voluntary private solutions are preferable has ideological roots in radical libertarian thought, it is not supported by mainstream research or governance practices due to its failure to address core societal needs and systemic inequities.

The Moral Illegitimacy of Taxation: A Form of State-Sanctioned Theft

At its heart, taxation is an egregious violation of individual liberty and property rights. Property rights—the cornerstone of a free society—dictate that individuals have the inherent right to the fruits of their labor. When a government imposes taxes, it forcibly seizes a portion of that property without the owner's voluntary agreement. This is not a voluntary transaction, like purchasing goods or services; it is coercion backed by the threat of fines, imprisonment, or even violence. As libertarian philosopher Murray Rothbard eloquently argued in his work For a New Liberty, taxation is "theft pure and simple," indistinguishable from a mugging except for the scale and legitimacy granted by the state.

If a private individual demanded a percentage of your income at gunpoint, we would rightly call it robbery. Why, then, do we accept the same behavior from the government? This double standard perpetuates a dangerous precedent, eroding the very foundation of justice. Taxation enables the state to grow unchecked, funding wars, surveillance, and wasteful bureaucracies that often serve elite interests rather than the public good. By abolishing taxation, we reclaim our autonomy and restore the moral order where individuals control their own resources, free from the state's predatory grasp.

Beyond its moral failings, taxation imposes severe economic costs that hinder individual and societal progress. Taxes distort market incentives, discouraging productivity and investment. When individuals and businesses know that a significant portion of their earnings will be confiscated, they are less motivated to work harder, innovate, or take risks. This phenomenon, known as the "deadweight loss" of taxation, reduces overall economic output and leads to inefficiencies. For instance, high income taxes can push talented entrepreneurs to relocate to low-tax jurisdictions, depriving their home countries of innovation and jobs.

History provides ample evidence of taxation's destructive effects. During the 20th century, countries like the Soviet Union and other communist regimes relied heavily on coercive taxation and state control, resulting in economic stagnation and widespread poverty. In contrast, free-market economies with minimal taxation, such as Hong Kong during its colonial period, experienced explosive growth. According to economic studies, such as those from the Cato Institute, excessive taxation correlates with lower GDP growth, reduced employment, and increased black-market activity. By eliminating taxes, we remove these barriers, allowing the free market to flourish. Individuals would retain more of their earnings, spurring investment in productive ventures and creating a more dynamic economy.

Bureaucrats and politicians allocate funds based on political expediency rather than merit, leading to bloated public sectors and misallocated resources. In a tax-free society, public services would need to compete in the marketplace, driving down costs and improving quality through innovation and accountability. This shift would not only boost economic growth but also empower individuals to direct their resources toward genuine societal needs.

Defense and public safety present another challenge, but even these can be handled privately. Healthcare, often cited as a reason for taxation, could be revolutionized through private charity and market competition. In reality, abolishing taxation would not lead to anarchy but to a more just and prosperous society. The state could transition to a minimal role, funded by user fees or voluntary contributions, ensuring stability without coercion.

Taxation is not a necessary evil; it is an evil that must be eradicated. As an illegitimate form of state theft, it violates moral principles, stifles economic growth, and perpetuates inefficiency. The Case for Abolition: Why Taxation Is Illegitimate and Why Voluntary Society Is Both Moral and Possible

Introduction

Few propositions in political life are treated with such unearned reverence as the claim that taxation is necessary, just, and beyond serious challenge. From childhood, citizens are taught that taxes are "the price we pay for civilization," a phrase attributed to Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr. that has functioned less as an argument and more as a conversation-stopper. Yet when examined with the same moral scrutiny we apply to every other human interaction, taxation reveals itself to be something remarkable: the one form of coercive extraction that polite society not only tolerates but celebrates. This essay argues that all forms of taxation—income, property, sales, capital gains, estate, excise, and every other permutation—should be completely abolished, and that every service currently funded through compulsory appropriation can and should be provided through voluntary means. This is not a radical proposition. It is simply the consistent application of moral principles that virtually everyone already holds.

I. The Moral Argument: Taxation as Institutionalized Theft

A. The Nature of the Act

Let us begin with a thought experiment that is disarmingly simple. Imagine your neighbor approaches you and demands $10,000. He explains that he intends to use this money for purposes he considers beneficial: paving your street, hiring a security guard for the neighborhood, and feeding a family on the next block. You may even agree that these are worthy goals. But you decline to contribute, or you wish to contribute a different amount, or you prefer a different street-paving company.

Your neighbor informs you that your preferences are irrelevant. If you do not surrender the money, he will send armed men to seize your property. If you resist the armed men, you will be placed in a cage. If you resist being placed in a cage, physical violence will escalate until you comply—or until you are dead.

No serious moral philosopher would hesitate to call this theft, extortion, or robbery. The worthiness of the neighbor's intended expenditure does not transform the nature of the act. As the philosopher Murray Rothbard observed, "Taxation is theft, purely and simply, even though it is theft on a grand and colossal scale which no acknowledged criminals could hope to match."

Now change one detail. Instead of your neighbor, the demand comes from an institution called "the government." The moral character of the interaction has not changed in any particular. The compulsion remains. The threat of violence remains. The irrelevance of your consent remains. The only thing that has changed is the scale and the social legitimacy conferred by tradition and repetition.

B. Consent and the Social Contract Fiction

The standard rejoinder is that citizens have "consented" to taxation through the social contract. This defense collapses under even gentle examination.

First, no citizen has ever signed a social contract. It is a metaphor elevated to the status of a binding legal instrument, which is philosophically absurd. As Lysander Spooner argued in No Treason (1870), the U.S. Constitution—the closest approximation to an explicit social contract in modern history—was signed by a small number of men, most of whom are now dead. It cannot bind those who never agreed to it any more than a contract your great-great-grandfather allegedly signed could bind you to mow a stranger's lawn in perpetuity.

Second, the argument that residence constitutes consent is circular. To say "you may leave if you don't like taxation" presupposes the government's legitimate authority over the territory—the very point in question. It is equivalent to a mafia boss telling a shopkeeper, "You consented to protection payments by choosing to open your shop in my territory." The shopkeeper's presence does not constitute consent; it merely reflects the practical difficulty of relocating one's life. Moreover, every inhabitable piece of land on Earth is claimed by some taxing government, leaving dissenters with no non-coercive jurisdiction to which they could emigrate. "Love it or leave it" is not a moral argument; it is a taunt.

Third, voting does not constitute consent to be taxed. One may vote defensively, attempting to minimize the coercion imposed upon oneself, without thereby endorsing the system that makes such defensive action necessary. A hostage who is permitted to vote on which captor holds the gun has not consented to captivity.

C. The Irrelevance of Majority Rule to Individual Rights

Democracy does not sanitize theft. If three people vote to take the fourth person's wallet, the act does not become legitimate by virtue of its democratic character. Rights, properly understood, are not subject to majority vote. The entire tradition of constitutional governance was ostensibly built to protect individual rights from majoritarian tyranny—yet taxation is the most pervasive and aggressive majoritarian imposition of all.

When abolitionists argued against slavery, they were not told, "But the majority supports it; you implicitly consented by living here." The moral invalidity of slavery did not depend on a vote count. Neither does the moral invalidity of forcibly appropriating a person's labor and property.

II. The Practical Destructiveness of Taxation

Even if one were to set aside the moral argument—which one should not—the practical consequences of taxation constitute a devastating indictment.

A. Economic Distortion and Deadweight Loss

Every tax levied creates what economists call "deadweight loss"—value destroyed through the distortion of voluntary exchange. When a transaction that would have been mutually beneficial does not occur because taxation has altered the cost-benefit calculus, wealth is not merely transferred; it is annihilated. Harvard economist Martin Feldstein estimated that the marginal deadweight loss of the U.S. income tax may exceed 30 cents per additional dollar raised. This means that for every dollar the government collects, society loses an additional thirty cents or more in unrealized economic activity.

Income taxes punish productive labor. Capital gains taxes punish investment. Corporate taxes punish enterprise. Property taxes punish ownership and stewardship. Estate taxes punish intergenerational wealth transfer and family continuity. Sales taxes punish consumption. At every stage of the economic cycle—earning, saving, investing, spending, and bequeathing—the state interposes itself to extract value and distort decisions. The cumulative effect is an economy operating perpetually below its potential, with millions of transactions foregone, businesses never started, inventions never pursued, and jobs never created.

B. Compliance Costs and Bureaucratic Waste

The Internal Revenue Service estimates that Americans spend over 6 billion hours annually on federal tax compliance. The Tax Foundation has estimated the compliance cost of the U.S. tax code at hundreds of billions of dollars per year. This represents an extraordinary diversion of human intelligence and labor into the purely parasitic activity of calculating, documenting, strategizing around, and litigating obligations to the state.

These are hours that doctors, engineers, teachers, and entrepreneurs could spend creating value. Instead, a vast industry of accountants, tax attorneys, compliance officers, and IRS agents exists for the sole purpose of navigating a labyrinth of coercive extraction. This is not a sign of civilization; it is a sign of profound institutional dysfunction.

C. Regulatory Capture and Crony Capitalism

Taxation funds a government apparatus that inevitably becomes the instrument of the politically connected. Public choice theory, pioneered by James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock, demonstrates that government actors are not benevolent Platonic guardians but self-interested agents who respond to incentives. The power to tax and spend creates a magnet for rent-seeking: industries lobby for subsidies, tariffs, and favorable regulations that are funded by tax dollars extracted from citizens who have no say in the resulting allocation.

The result is not a fair distribution of public goods but a system in which the politically powerful plunder the politically weak. Abolishing taxation would eliminate the honey pot that attracts this corruption.

D. The Ratchet Effect and Government Growth

Robert Higgs's "ratchet effect" demonstrates that government grows during crises and never fully contracts afterward. Each war, recession, and emergency becomes a pretext for new taxes and new spending that become permanent features of the fiscal landscape. Taxation is not a stable, controlled mechanism; it is a one-way valve through which liberty drains. The U.S. federal income tax, introduced in 1913 at a marginal rate of 7%, reached 94% within three decades. What begins as modest invariably becomes monstrous.

III. The Viable Alternative: Voluntary Funding and Private Provision

The most frequent objection to abolishing taxation is: "But who will build the roads? Who will fund the military? Who will care for the poor?" These objections, though understandable, reflect a profound failure of imagination—and an ignorance of both history and existing private-sector achievements.

A. Private Provision of Infrastructure

Roads, the perennial trump card of tax advocates, were historically built and maintained privately. The turnpike trusts of 18th- and 19th-century Britain and early America constructed thousands of miles of roads funded by voluntary toll payments from users. Modern technology makes this even more feasible: electronic tolling, GPS-based road pricing, and subscription models can fund road construction and maintenance through direct user fees rather than coercive extraction from the general population—including those who rarely use the roads in question.

Private companies already build and operate highways, bridges, airports, seaports, water systems, and electrical grids around the world. The Channel Tunnel, connecting England and France, was built entirely with private capital. The notion that infrastructure requires taxation is not an empirical observation; it is an article of faith.

B. Private Security and Defense

Private security is already a larger industry than public policing in many countries. In the United States, private security guards outnumber public police officers by approximately three to one. Gated communities, private arbitration services, and neighborhood associations demonstrate that people voluntarily fund their own protection when given the opportunity.

National defense presents a more complex challenge, often framed through the "public goods" problem of non-excludability and free riding. Yet several responses are available:

  1. Voluntary defense associations: Historical examples include the Swiss militia tradition, in which citizens voluntarily armed and organized for common defense, without the need for a coercive tax-funded standing army.

  2. Subscription and insurance models: Defense could be funded through voluntary subscription services or bundled into property and business insurance. Insurers have powerful incentives to prevent large-scale destruction of the assets they insure and could coordinate and fund defensive capabilities accordingly.

  3. Crowdfunding and philanthropy: In the modern era, voluntary collective funding mechanisms are more powerful than ever. If citizens are willing to donate billions annually to charities, universities, and disaster relief, the notion that they would refuse to fund their own defense is implausible.

  4. Decreased need for military expenditure: A substantial portion of current military spending funds offensive foreign interventions and global empire-maintenance that actually increase the threats citizens face. A purely defensive posture, organized voluntarily, would require a fraction of current expenditure.

C. Private Charity and Mutual Aid

The claim that without taxation, the poor would starve, is refuted by both logic and history. Americans voluntarily donate over $500 billion to charity annually—and this figure exists despite the enormous tax burden that reduces disposable income and despite the crowding-out effect whereby government welfare programs diminish the perceived need for private charity.

Before the modern welfare state, an extraordinary network of mutual aid societies, fraternal organizations, churches, and charitable institutions served the poor, the sick, and the elderly. Historian David Beito's From Mutual Aid to the Welfare State documents how fraternal societies provided healthcare, life insurance, orphan care, and elderly support to millions of working-class Americans—including African Americans and immigrants excluded from government programs.

These voluntary institutions were systematically displaced not because they failed, but because the state regulated, taxed, and outcompeted them with "free" services funded by compulsion. Abolishing taxation would unleash a renaissance of voluntary mutual aid, with the added advantages of local knowledge, accountability, compassion, and genuine community bonds that bureaucratic welfare programs notoriously lack.

D. Dispute Resolution and Law

Private arbitration already resolves the majority of commercial disputes in the United States. Organizations like the American Arbitration Association and JAMS handle hundreds of thousands of cases annually, often more quickly, cheaply, and satisfactorily than government courts. International commercial law operates largely through private arbitration under frameworks like the ICC Rules.

A fully voluntary society could sustain sophisticated legal institutions through subscription-based courts, reputational enforcement mechanisms, and private contract law—as explored in detail by legal theorists such as Bruce Benson (The Enterprise of Law) and David Friedman (The Machinery of Freedom).

E. Education

Private and homeschool education consistently outperforms government schools on nearly every metric. The government monopoly on education—funded by taxation—has produced stagnant outcomes despite exponentially increasing per-pupil expenditure. Voluntary funding through tuition, scholarships, endowments, and philanthropic foundations would create a competitive, innovative, accountable education market that serves students rather than bureaucracies and teachers' unions.

IV. Addressing Common Objections

A. "Free Rider Problems Make Voluntary Funding Impossible"

The free rider problem is real but routinely overstated. First, many "public goods" are not truly non-excludable; technology increasingly enables exclusion (encryption, electronic access, GPS tracking). Second, social norms, reputational incentives, and community pressure powerfully motivate contribution even absent excludability. Third, the existence of free riders does not justify coercion any more than the existence of lying justifies compulsory truth serum. The moral prohibition on theft does not contain a utilitarian exception clause.

B. "Without Taxation, Only the Rich Would Have Services"

This inverts the reality. Taxation is profoundly regressive in practice if not in nominal rate structure. Compliance complexity favors the wealthy, who can afford sophisticated tax planning. Government services disproportionately benefit the politically connected—corporate subsidies, defense contracts, regulatory barriers that protect incumbents from competition. The poor pay sales taxes, payroll taxes, and the hidden tax of inflation, while receiving services of notoriously poor quality.

A voluntary system would empower the poor by eliminating the tax burden on their labor and consumption, lowering prices through deregulated competition, and channeling aid through accountable, compassionate private institutions rather than indifferent bureaucracies.

C. "This Has Never Been Tried on a Large Scale"

The abolition of slavery had not been tried on a large scale either, prior to the 19th century. "It has never been done" is a counsel of despair, not an argument of principle. Moreover, large portions of the modern economy already operate on voluntary principles. The technology sector, international commerce, charitable giving, private education, private healthcare, and private security all demonstrate that voluntary cooperation can achieve extraordinary scale and complexity.

D. "Some Things Are Too Important to Leave to Voluntary Action"

This argument is precisely backwards. The more important a good or service is—food, healthcare, education, security—the more dangerous it is to entrust its provision to a coercive monopoly insulated from competition and consumer choice. We do not nationalize food production because food is important; the countries that tried—the Soviet Union, Maoist China, North Korea—produced famine. Importance is an argument for market provision, not against it.

V. The Philosophical Stakes

The debate over taxation is ultimately a debate over the nature of the individual's relationship to the state. There are only two coherent positions:

  1. The individual is sovereign. She owns her body, her labor, and the fruits of her labor. No person or institution may take her property without her consent. This is the principle of self-ownership, and it is the foundation of every prohibition against assault, slavery, and theft that civilization recognizes.

  2. The state is sovereign. The individual's property belongs ultimately to the collective, and the state permits her to retain whatever portion it sees fit. Her labor is subject to conscription-by-percentage. She is, in the precise and limited sense relevant here, a serf—permitted to work the land but required to remit a share of the harvest to the lord.

There is no middle ground. Any percentage of taxation, however small, concedes the principle that the state has a prior claim on your labor. If the government may take 30%, why not 50%? If 50%, why not 70%? If there is no principled limit—and no tax advocate has ever articulated one grounded in anything more than political expediency—then the logical terminus is 100%, which is slavery.

The abolition of taxation is the assertion that the terminus lies at the other end: at zero. It is the assertion that you own yourself completely, that your labor is yours, that your life is yours, and that no collective—however large, however democratic, however well-intentioned—may claim otherwise.

Conclusion

The abolition of all taxation is not a utopian fantasy. It is the logical extension of the moral principles we already accept in every other domain of life. We do not tolerate theft between individuals; we should not tolerate it between the state and the individual. We do not accept that good intentions justify coercion in personal relationships; we should not accept it in political relationships. We recognize that voluntary cooperation produces better outcomes than compulsion in markets, in charity, in education, and in virtually every realm of human endeavor; we should recognize it in the provision of public services as well.

The question is not whether we can afford to abolish taxation. The question is whether we can afford—morally, economically, and philosophically—to continue pretending that an institution built on coercion, sustained by threats, and executed through violence is the foundation of a free and civilized society. It is not. It is the most enduring and most dangerous relic of an age that believed human beings were subjects rather than sovereigns.

Taxation should be abolished—not reformed, not simplified, not reduced—abolished. And in its place, the extraordinary, creative, compassionate power of free human beings, cooperating voluntarily, should be trusted to build the civilization we deserve.

"If taxation without consent is robbery, the United States government has never had, has not now, and is never likely to have, a single honest dollar in its treasury." — Lysander Spooner, No Treason (1870)

The Case for Voluntary Society

A Speech on Taxation and Liberty

Friends, fellow citizens, believers in human dignity —

I stand before you today to voice a conviction that many of you feel in your bones but have been told is impractical, radical, or naive. I'm here to tell you it is none of those things. It is, in fact, the most honest position in political life.

Taxation, as we know it, is compulsion. Let us not dress it in softer language. When an institution says, "Give us a portion of what you have earned, or we will fine you, seize your property, and ultimately cage you," that is not a voluntary arrangement. That is not consent. No amount of civic ritual changes the fundamental nature of the act.

If your neighbor came to your door and demanded thirty percent of your paycheck — even if he promised to fix the road and fund a school — you would call it what it is. The badge of the state does not transform the ethics of the exchange.

The Consent That Never Was

We are told we "consent" to taxation through democracy. But let us examine that claim honestly.

Did you sign a contract? Were you presented with terms you could negotiate, accept, or walk away from? Can you opt out if you disagree with how your money is spent — on wars you oppose, on subsidies to corporations you find repugnant, on bureaucracies that serve themselves more than they serve you?

You cannot. You were born into this arrangement. You inherited obligations you never chose. Lysander Spooner observed over a century ago that the Constitution is a document no living person signed, yet it is used to justify claims on the fruits of your labor from your first paycheck to your last breath — and even beyond, in the form of estate taxes on wealth already taxed.

Consent that cannot be withdrawn is not consent at all.

The Moral Foundation

Let me be clear about the principle at stake. I believe — and I suspect many of you believe — in a simple moral axiom:

No person has the right to take another person's property by force.

This is not a complicated idea. Children understand it. Every legal and moral system in history recognizes theft as wrong. We simply ask that this principle be applied consistently — to individuals, to groups, and yes, to governments.

Some will say, "But government provides services!" And I will answer: so does every business on earth. The difference is that every other provider of goods and services must earn your patronage. They must offer you value sufficient that you willingly part with your money. Only government exempts itself from this standard. Only government says, "You will pay, whether you wish to or not, whether you find our service satisfactory or not, whether you use it or not."

This is not a service model. It is a monopoly enforced by coercion.

The Practical Case

Now, I know what the skeptics among you are thinking. "Fine, the philosophy is compelling. But would it work?"

Let me ask you this: Does the current system work?

Are your roads without potholes? Are your schools producing excellence? Is your healthcare affordable? Is your government fiscally responsible? Are the trillions extracted from working people year after year producing outcomes that justify the extraction?

The national debt alone tells you the answer. Government doesn't just take what you produce today — it borrows against what your children and grandchildren will produce, spending their labor before they've drawn their first working breath. If that is the "responsible" system, I shudder to think what irresponsibility looks like.

Now consider what voluntary systems have already achieved — even while forced to compete against tax-funded monopolies:

Private charity and mutual aid built hospitals, libraries, schools, fire companies, and community infrastructure long before the modern tax state. In the 19th century, fraternal societies provided healthcare, life insurance, and social safety nets to millions of working-class Americans — through voluntary association, without a single dollar of compulsory taxation.

Open-source collaboration has produced software that runs most of the internet — created by people contributing freely because they choose to, because they see the value.

Crowdfunding has financed medical treatments, disaster relief, scientific research, and creative endeavors — millions of people giving freely because they believe in the cause.

Voluntary subscription services today provide security, education, communication, transportation, and dispute resolution — often more efficiently and responsively than their government counterparts.

The question is not whether people will fund the things they value. Of course they will. The question is whether you trust free people to make those decisions, or whether you believe they must be forced.

A Vision for Voluntary Funding

What would a system based on voluntary contribution look like?

Imagine communities where every service — roads, defense, dispute resolution, education, environmental protection — must earn its funding by demonstrating value to the people it serves.

Imagine a world where:

  • You choose which community services receive your support, creating real accountability
  • Entrepreneurs and nonprofits compete to solve public problems, driving innovation instead of bureaucratic stagnation
  • User fees and subscriptions fund infrastructure, paid by those who use it, proportional to their use
  • Mutual aid societies and voluntary insurance cooperatives provide safety nets built on genuine solidarity rather than compulsory redistribution
  • Community associations and contractual governance replace top-down mandates with bottom-up agreement
  • Philanthropy and endowment fund research, education, and the arts — as they already do to a remarkable degree even within the current system

Would this require cultural change? Of course. But every great expansion of human freedom required cultural change. The abolition of slavery required it. The recognition of individual rights required it. Every time we have moved away from coercion and toward consent, prophets of doom predicted chaos — and every time, free people proved them wrong.

Answering the Objections

"But what about the poor?"

I care about the poor. That is precisely why I oppose a system where political insiders and well-connected corporations capture the vast majority of tax revenue, where regulatory barriers protect incumbents from competition, where inflation — the hidden tax — devastates the purchasing power of those on fixed incomes, and where dependency is incentivized over self-determination.

Voluntary societies throughout history have shown extraordinary generosity. Americans alone give over $500 billion annually to charity — under a system that already takes trillions in taxes. Imagine what a society would give if people retained the full fruit of their labor and internalized the full responsibility for their communities.

"But what about defense?"

Throughout history, people have voluntarily organized to defend their communities, their families, and their property. The question is whether defense must be funded through compulsion or whether people who genuinely value their security — and they do — will fund it voluntarily. I believe they will, and I believe the result will be defense that serves the people rather than the ambitions of political leaders.

"But what about free riders?"

Free riders exist in every system — including the current one, where politically connected entities consume far more in government benefits than they contribute in taxes. The difference is that voluntary systems develop organic mechanisms to address free-riding: social pressure, reputation systems, contractual arrangements, and exclusion from benefits. These are the tools of cooperation. Compulsion is the tool of domination.

The Deeper Truth

Friends, this is ultimately not an argument about policy. It is an argument about what kind of beings we believe humans are.

If you believe people are fundamentally incapable of organizing themselves, incapable of generosity, incapable of cooperation without the threat of imprisonment — then by all means, support the coercive state. But then ask yourself: if people are so selfish and shortsighted, why would you trust those same people with the coercive power of government?

If, on the other hand, you believe — as I do — that human beings are capable of extraordinary cooperation, creativity, and compassion when they are free — then the case for compulsory taxation collapses under the weight of its own contradictions.

Every dollar taken by force is a dollar that could have been invested, donated, spent, or saved according to the judgment of the person who earned it. Every act of compulsory redistribution is a statement that the political class knows better than you how to allocate the resources you created through your labor, your ingenuity, and your sacrifice.

I reject that premise. I reject it completely.

The Call

I am not calling for chaos. I am calling for order — the organic, emergent, extraordinary order that arises when free people are permitted to cooperate without coercion. The order of markets, of voluntary associations, of communities built on genuine consent.

I am calling for a society where every interaction is voluntary. Where every contribution is chosen. Where every institution earns its support rather than extracting it at gunpoint.

I am calling for the radical, beautiful, revolutionary idea that your life belongs to you. That the fruits of your labor belong to you. That no one — no king, no congress, no majority — has the right to take them without your consent.

This is not a new idea. It is the oldest idea in the human yearning for freedom. It is the idea that launched revolutions and toppled empires. It is the idea that slavery is wrong — not just chattel slavery, but the partial slavery of compulsory labor for the benefit of others.

If you believe in human dignity — truly believe in it — then stand with me. Stand for consent. Stand for voluntarism. Stand for the radical proposition that free people, left to their own devices, will build a world more just, more prosperous, and more compassionate than any coercive system could ever achieve.

The future belongs to freedom — if we have the courage to claim it.

Thank you.
